title: Zechariah 2:1–13
context: Versification: English 1:18–21 is Hebrew 2:1–4, and English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:5–17; this page keeps the WEB numbers. In the third night vision the prophet sees a man with a measuring line going to measure Jerusalem (2:1–2). Another angel sends word that Jerusalem will be inhabited like villages without walls because of its many people and livestock, for the LORD says he will be “a wall of fire around it” and “the glory in the middle of her” (2:3–5). An oracle follows, calling exiles to flee the land of the north and Babylon (2:6–7), promising judgment on the plunderers, for “he who touches you touches the apple of his eye” (2:8–9), and calling Zion to sing because the LORD comes to dwell in her (2:10). Many nations will join themselves to the LORD (2:11), the LORD will again choose Jerusalem (2:12), and all flesh is told to be silent before him (2:13). The voice that says “the LORD of Armies has sent me” (2:9, 11) is read as the prophet, as the angel of the LORD, or as a messianic figure, and these notes keep the question open. Measuring scenes also appear in Ezekiel 40 and Revelation 11 and 21; they are named here without merging. Shared ground: both traditions read the wall of fire and the call to sing and rejoice as a promise of the LORD’s protecting presence among his people.

verses.text: I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, a man with a measuring line in his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet sees a man with a measuring line in his hand. Arminian readers see the third vision opening with an image of planning and building, fitting for a community rebuilding Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel with measuring scenes in Ezekiel 40:3 and Revelation 11:1 and 21:15, named by reference without merging. Both traditions read the measuring line as connected to restoration, picking up 1:16.

verses.text: Then I asked, “Where are you going?” He said to me, “To measure Jerusalem, to see what is its width and what is its length.”
verses.arminianNotes: The man says he is going to measure Jerusalem’s width and length. Arminian readers see an attempt to define the city’s limits, which the following verses will expand beyond expectation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the measuring as preparing for the revelation that the city will exceed any human boundary. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as setting up a contrast between human measurement and God’s larger plan.

verses.text: Behold, the angel who talked with me went out, and another angel went out to meet him,
verses.arminianNotes: The interpreting angel goes out, and another angel comes to meet him. Arminian readers see the heavenly messengers active in carrying God’s word, a sign of divine attention to Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the second angel is introduced without a name, and readers identify him in different ways. Both traditions read the meeting as advancing the vision toward its central message about Jerusalem.

verses.text: and said to him, “Run, speak to this young man, saying, ‘Jerusalem will be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of men and livestock in it.
verses.arminianNotes: The angel says Jerusalem will be inhabited like villages without walls because of its many people and animals. Arminian readers see overflowing growth that walls cannot contain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise of abundance exceeding the measured boundaries. Shared ground: both traditions read unwalled villages as a picture of peace and plenty, and they note the young man may be the measurer or the prophet.

verses.text: For I,’ says the LORD, ‘will be to her a wall of fire around it, and I will be the glory in the middle of her.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will be a wall of fire around Jerusalem and the glory in her midst. Arminian readers see God’s presence as the true security of his people, greater than any stone wall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the echo of the pillar of fire, compare Exodus 13:21 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the wall of fire and the glory within as a promise of the LORD’s protecting and dwelling presence.

verses.text: Come! Come! Flee from the land of the north,’ says the LORD; ‘for I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the sky,’ says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls, Come! Flee from the land of the north, for he has spread them as the four winds. Arminian readers see an urgent invitation to exiles still in Babylon to return home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign hand both in scattering and in regathering. Both traditions read the land of the north as Babylon, from which invaders came, and they hear the call as urgent and hopeful.

verses.text: ‘Come, Zion! Escape, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.’
verses.arminianNotes: Come, Zion! Escape, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. Arminian readers see the call extended personally to those who remained in exile, urging them to leave.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the daughter of Babylon as a personified city whose hold on the exiles is now broken. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a summons to leave exile behind and join the community rebuilding Zion.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies says: ‘For honor he has sent me to the nations which plundered you; for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says he has been sent to the nations that plundered them, for whoever touches them touches the apple of his eye. Arminian readers see God’s tender protection of his people, compare Deuteronomy 32:10 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image in Psalm 17:8 and see God’s covenant care. Both traditions read the apple of his eye as an image of what is most precious and protected, and they hold the identity of the one sent openly.

verses.text: For, behold, I will shake my hand over them, and they will be a plunder to those who served them; and you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will shake his hand over the plunderers, and they will become plunder to those who served them. Arminian readers see a reversal of fortunes, as oppressors become the oppressed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s power to judge with a mere gesture. Shared ground: both traditions read the vindication of the messenger, you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me, as confirming God’s word.

verses.text: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion! For behold, I come and I will dwell within you,’ says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for the LORD comes to dwell within her. Arminian readers see joyful worship as the response to God’s promised presence, compare Zephaniah 3:14 by reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise of God dwelling among his people as the heart of covenant hope. Shared ground: both traditions read the call to sing as rejoicing in the LORD’s presence, a theme fulfilled in various ways in Scripture.

verses.text: Many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people; and I will dwell among you, and you shall know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you.
verses.arminianNotes: Many nations will join themselves to the LORD and become his people. Arminian readers see the wideness of God’s welcome, open to all nations who come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God gathering a people from the nations according to his purpose, compare Isaiah 2:2–3 and Zechariah 8:22–23 by reference. Both traditions read the verse with joy at the inclusion of the nations, and they hold its fulfillment details with care.

verses.text: The LORD will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land, and will again choose Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land and again choose Jerusalem. Arminian readers see God’s renewed commitment to his people and place after the exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the striking phrase the holy land, which marks the territory as set apart for God because he claims it as his own. Shared ground: both traditions read again choose as renewed covenant favor, echoing 1:17.

verses.text: Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD; for he has roused himself from his holy habitation!”
verses.arminianNotes: All flesh is told to be silent before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy habitation. Arminian readers see reverent awe as the fitting response when God acts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the close parallel with Habakkuk 2:20 by reference, calling the earth to silence before God. Both traditions read the verse as closing the vision with reverence before the LORD who is about to act.
